coreTruths.title: Valid consent is voluntary, ongoing, capacity-based, and tailored to what matters to this patient
coreTruths.broaderContext: Consent is the legal floor under every clinical contact. Get it wrong and routine treatment becomes assault, negligence, or a fitness to practise issue.
coreTruths.body:
## Consent is a continuous conversation, not a signature

Valid consent means a capable patient voluntarily agreeing to a specific treatment after being told its purpose, nature, likely risks, chance of success, and alternatives [1]. It runs through the whole course of treatment, not just the moment a form is signed. A signed form is not proof of valid consent if the patient never really understood or had time to weigh things up [2].

## Treatment with no consent is assault, with poor consent is negligence

These are two separate failures. Treating without any consent is assault or battery. Treating with general consent but no proper explanation can amount to negligence [3]. So the question is never just "did they say yes" but "did they say yes to this, knowing what this involved".

## Material risk is what matters to this patient, not the textbook list

Since Montgomery v Lanarkshire, the clinician has to discuss risks that are material to the individual in front of them, not just risks that are material on average [4]. A trumpeter contemplating IDB needs the lip paraesthesia conversation in a way another patient might not. That only works if there is enough rapport and curiosity to know what would change the patient's mind [4].

## Implied consent stops at the examination

Sitting in the chair counts as implied consent to be looked at. It does not cover any treatment [5]. Anything beyond examination needs explicit consent, with written consent the legal requirement for sedation or GA [6].

citations.quote: Valid consent is the voluntary and continuous permission of a capable patient to receive a particular treatment based on the patient being informed regarding the purpose, nature, and likely risks of the treatment, including the likelihood of its success and any alternatives to it. Permission given under any unfair or undue pressure is not consent.

A signed form indicating that a patient agrees to treatment is not necessarily proof that consent is valid because the patient may not have understood the information provided at the time they gave their consent, or they may not have had enough information to make a proper decision, or enough time to consider their options.
Treatment without any consent = assault/battery. Treatment with general consent, but without explanation of what is involved may = negligence.

The ruling in Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11 declares that a material risk to that patient has to be considered when consenting a patient. This means that while it might not be necessarily a relevant (or material) risk to all patients undergoing the same procedure, in that particular case it may be a significant material risk to that patient, and therefore would determine if they undergo the procedure or not.
Implied consent to a dental examination is given by attending an appointment and sitting in the dental chair; however, this does not cover provision of treatment.
It is a legal requirement for treatment involving conscious impairment such as sedation or GA.

coreTruths.title: Capacity is presumed in adults and judged on a defined functional test, not on the decision itself
coreTruths.broaderContext: How a clinician handles capacity decides whether treatment is lawful or unlawful. The starting position is presumption of capacity, with a fixed functional test if it is in doubt.
coreTruths.body:
## Adults are presumed to have capacity until shown otherwise

The Mental Capacity Act starting position is that a patient over 16 is assumed capable of consenting unless proved otherwise [1]. Capacity is decision-specific, so a patient may be capable for a simple decision and not for a complex one.

## Capacity is a five-part functional test

Capacity to consent rests on whether the patient can understand the information, retain it, weigh it up, ask for more if needed, and communicate their decision [2]. A refusal that looks unwise is not the same as lacking capacity. The test is about the process of deciding, not the outcome.

## No one consents for an incapacitated adult unless there is an LPA

Under common law, no one can consent on behalf of an adult who lacks capacity. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 created the lasting power of attorney as the route around this, set up while the patient still has capacity [3]. Without an LPA, treatment can still go ahead if it is in the patient's best interests and there is no valid advance refusal [4].

## Best interests is a structured judgement, not a clinician's gut feel

A best-interests decision means involving the patient as far as possible, mapping their past and present views, beliefs and values, avoiding discrimination, asking whether capacity might return so treatment can wait, and consulting carers, relatives, or any LPA [5]. The treating clinician carries the final call [6], but only after that process.

## Children: 16 and 17 are presumed competent, younger children can be Gillick competent

For 16- and 17-year-olds the presumption mirrors adults. Younger children who genuinely understand the procedure can consent themselves under Gillick competence, and a parent cannot override that consent [7]. Where the child cannot consent, someone with parental responsibility must, and the responsibility status of fathers, grandparents and carers should be checked rather than assumed [8].

citations.quote: The Mental Health Act7 requires that it should be assumed that a patient over age 16yrs has the capacity to consent to treatment unless proved otherwise.

Capacity to consent to treatment is based upon whether a patient can: Understand information provided regarding the proposed care. Retain the information provided. Use or weigh that information as part of the process of making the decision. Ask for further information if they need to, before reaching their decision. Communicate the decision (whether by talking, using sign language, or by any other means).

Under common law, no person can consent for a patient who lacks mental capacity; however, the Mental Capacity Act 20058 enables an individual with capacity to give another individual a lasting power of attorney (LPA) to make medical decisions on their behalf should their capacity become impaired.

Where no LPA exists, a patient lacking capacity may receive treatment necessary to preserve life, health, or well-being provided that the treatment is in the best interests of the patient and no valid ‘advance refusal’ exists.

When considering whether treatment is in a patient’s best interests: Encourage the person to take part in the decision. Identify all relevant circumstances (what the person would take into account if they had capacity), e.g. past/present views, beliefs/values (religious/cultural). Avoid discrimination. Assess whether the patient may regain capacity at a later time (this is relevant if treatment can be deferred until then). Consult others, e.g. anyone involved in caring for the patient, close relatives, LPA, deputy appointed by Court of Protection.
The final ‘decision-maker’ regarding healthcare rests with the doctor/healthcare worker responsible for carrying out the particular treatment.

Those aged 16yrs and 17yrs are presumed to have the competence to give consent for their own treatment. Younger children who understand fully what is involved in the proposed procedure can also give consent (although their parents will ideally be involved). In other cases, someone with parental responsibility must give consent on the child’s behalf, unless they cannot be reached in an emergency. If a competent child consents to treatment, a parent cannot override that consent (the ‘Gillick competence’ principle).

It is important to check that a person providing consent for a child’s treatment has parental responsibility to do so. A child’s mother will automatically have parental responsibility (unless this has been removed by a court). A father may not, depending upon his relationship with the mother at the time the child was born and whether his name appears on the birth certificate.

coreTruths.title: Negligence is a three-element framework: duty, breach, and damage caused by that breach
coreTruths.broaderContext: Negligence claims are how dentistry is most often held to legal account. Knowing the framework points directly at the daily habits that prevent claims succeeding.
coreTruths.body:
## A claim only succeeds if all three elements are proved

Professional negligence is a failure to exercise reasonable care, in a professional capacity, that results in harm [1]. The claimant has to prove a duty of care was owed, that duty was breached, and damage was caused as a direct result of that breach [2]. Miss any one and the claim fails. No demonstrable harm means no case in negligence, even if the care was poor [3].

## Reasonable care is set by Bolam, then sense-checked by Bolitho

What counts as reasonable care turns on what a responsible body of similar clinicians would do (Bolam). If that body's practice is illogical, the court can still find negligence even when other clinicians would have done the same (Bolitho) [4]. So defending care by saying "plenty of dentists do it this way" is not a guaranteed shield.

## Vicarious liability extends a dentist's exposure beyond their own hands

An employer is responsible for the negligence of an employee during their employment [5]. That covers nurses and receptionists, and increasingly applies to people working under a clinician's direction even when not formally employed [5]. Each individual is also liable for their own acts, so claims can run against both.

## Records and saying sorry are the two practical defences

Clear, contemporaneous records are the single most important piece of evidence that appropriate care was given [6]. Records must never be altered or rewritten after a complaint, only added to with a clear date and initials [7]. Saying sorry that an incident has happened is not an admission of guilt, fault or liability [8], so the instinct to apologise does not need to be suppressed.

## The clock starts when the patient knew or should have known

Time bar for negligence is usually three years, but it does not start running until the patient knew, or should have known, of the damage [9]. For children it starts at 18, and there is no time bar for those with mental disability [9]. So records have to be kept long enough to defend a claim that may surface years later.

citations.quote: Professional negligence is defined as a failure to exercise reasonable care, in one’s professional capacity, which results in a patient suffering harm.

For a negligence case to win, the onus is on the claimant to prove: The dentist owed a duty of care to the patient. There was a breach of that duty. Damage occurred to the claimant as a direct result of that breach.
Where no demonstrable loss has occurred, a patient has no recourse in the law but may still voice a complaint to a regulatory body or via the practice complaints procedure.

Often negligence cases hinge on what constitutes ‘reasonable care’. If a dentist can show that their actions were in line with those of a large number of their colleagues, he/she is unlikely to be held negligent (Bolam test). However, if those actions were deemed to be illogical by the court, negligence may well be found in that situation even if others may have done the same (Bolitho test).

An employer can be held responsible for any negligence by an employee that occurs during their employ. This means that a dentist is responsible for the actions or omissions of their staff, e.g. dental nurse, receptionist. However, as every individual is responsible for their own acts, a charge of negligence could be brought against both employee and employer. It is also possible to be held vicariously liable for acts and omissions of somebody who you do not employ if it can be demonstrated that an individual was acting under your control/direction, e.g. this could apply to self-employed members of the team.

The importance of clear, concise, and contemporaneous notes cannot be over-emphasized. Good-quality record cards, radiographs, photographs, and study models (where appropriate) are invaluable in supplying evidence to support that appropriate care was provided.

When a complaint is received, deficiencies in records may be identified; however, never alter, amend, or rewrite the records. Any additions to a record should be clearly initialled and dated at the time the entry was made.

when complications and errors do arise, you should be prepared to give your patients factual information about what has happened in a caring and supportive fashion. Saying that you are sorry that an incident has occurred is not necessarily an admission of guilt, fault or liability

The period of limitation during which a patient must bring a claim is usually 3yrs but this does not begin to run until the patient knows, or ought to have known, of the damage that is said to have occurred. For children, the time bar does not start until 18yrs of age; there is no time bar in the case of mental disability.

coreTruths.title: Confidentiality is the default, with narrow and justified exceptions
coreTruths.broaderContext: Patients only share what they share because they trust it stays with the team. That trust is a regulated professional duty, not just a courtesy.
coreTruths.body:
## Confidentiality is a GDC-level duty, not a soft promise

A core GDC principle is that information about patients is treated as confidential and used only for the purpose for which it was given [1]. That covers everything from medical history to photos. Casual disclosures, even to other patients or family members, breach this duty.

## Exceptions are narrow and have to be justified

Breach of confidentiality is only justified in exceptional circumstances, in the patient's interest or the public interest [1]. So the bar for releasing information is high and the reasoning has to be defensible.

## Police requests are not automatic permission to disclose

A registrant has a duty to protect confidentiality. Even when the police ask for information, advice should be sought from a defence society before releasing anything [2]. Information can be disclosed if a Court Order is obtained [2], which is the route that puts the decision on a legal footing rather than a clinical one.

## Photographs and identifiable images need their own written authority

Using patient photographs for a lecture or presentation needs written authority confirming the patient understands how and when the images will be used [3]. Consent for the procedure does not cover later use of images.

citations.quote: Treat information about patients as confidential and only use it for the purpose for which it is given. Breach of confidentiality may be justified only in exceptional circumstances if in the patient’s or public interest.

Occasionally, a practitioner may be requested by the police to release confidential information. The advice of a defence society should be sought before a decision is made to release any information. A registrant has a duty to protect confidentiality. Information may be disclosed if a Court Order is obtained.
If a patient’s photographs are to be used for a lecture or presentation, written authority to do so should be obtained from the patient confirming their understanding of how/when images will be used.

coreTruths.title: Fitness to practise and negligence are separate systems with different aims
coreTruths.broaderContext: These are the two main routes a clinician can be held to account. Confusing them leads to defending the wrong thing in the wrong forum.
coreTruths.body:
## Negligence is about righting a wrong; fitness to practise is about protecting the public

A fitness to practise proceeding is not a court case for negligence. Negligence law exists to compensate harm. Fitness to practise exists to keep the public safe [1]. So a registrant can be found negligent without it being a fitness to practise issue, and can face a fitness to practise issue without any negligent act [1].

## The same incident can spawn both, in either order

A fitness to practise proceeding can lead to a negligence claim, and a negligence claim can trigger a fitness to practise proceeding [1]. They run on separate timelines with separate evidence thresholds, so handling one well does not close the other.

## Fitness to practise covers more than clinical performance

Impairment can be alleged through misconduct (professional or personal, including convictions or cautions in the UK or elsewhere), deficient performance, or adverse health [2]. So personal-life conduct and health issues, not just clinical ones, can put registration at risk.

## A criminal conviction, even unrelated to dentistry, threatens registration

A registrant risks erasure for any criminal conviction, even one unrelated to professional practice or predating registration [3]. A guilty plea or accepting a caution counts as an admission of guilt to the GDC [3]. So legal advice on a criminal matter is also a registration matter.

## Indemnity is mandatory and has to fit the actual scope of work

All GDC registrants must have adequate, appropriate indemnity so patients can be compensated if they are entitled to it [4]. NHS/Crown indemnity covers NHS work but not private treatment, regulatory issues, fatal accident enquiries, or coroner's inquests [5], so anyone doing private work or stepping outside core NHS care needs separate cover. Insurance run-off cover is what protects against claims that arrive after a policy has ended [6].

citations.quote: It is important to remember that a fitness to practise proceeding is not the same as a court case for negligence. It is possible to be negligent in the eyes of the law but this would not necessarily be a GDC fitness to practise matter, and likewise it could be that there is a fitness to practise matter that does not hinge on a negligent act. These are two separate entities: negligence is purely about righting a wrong, whereas fitness to practise is about protecting the public. However, a fitness to practise proceeding may also lead to a claim being made for negligence, and vice versa.

Fitness to practise may be alleged to be impaired due to: Misconduct, either professional or personal, including convictions/cautions received in UK or elsewhere. Deficient professional performance. Adverse health.

A dentist or DCP may risk having their name erased from the register if they are convicted of a criminal offence (even if unrelated to professional practice or arising from a time prior to registration) or it is found that their fitness to practise is impaired. If a registrant enters a plea of guilty in a criminal matter or accepts a caution for a charge, this will be taken as an admission of guilt by the GDC.
All GDC registrants are required to have adequate and appropriate indemnity cover to ensure that patients can claim compensation if they are entitled to it.

Crown/NHS indemnity provides cover relating to acts or omissions of doctors and dentists working in NHS hospitals and salaried 1° care. Crown/NHS indemnity covers work undertaken within the NHS contract; it does not provide assistance for private treatment, regulatory issues (GDC/General Medical Council), fatal accident enquiries, or coroner’s inquest.

Insurance-based indemnity provides cover for claims arising during the period that the policy is in force. ‘Run-off’ cover may also need to be purchased to cover claims arising outside of the insurance term if changing indemnity provider or retiring.
